Problem 7.31 Lesson 17 · p. 479 · §7.2

Voltage gain of a MOSFET amplifier with a drain-to-gate resistor, including the finite output resistance, at two bias currents.

Problem statement

7.31 In the circuit of Fig. P7.31, the NMOS transistor has |Vt|=0.8 V and VA=20 V and operates with VD=1 V. What is the voltage gain vo/vi? What do VD and the gain become for I increased to 1 mA?

The problem is marked with the simulation icon SIM and the video-example icon VE 7.1 (the same circuit, p. 393).

Expansion note: how to read the capacitors and the current source in this circuit

The infinity symbols on the capacitors mean they are large enough to act as short circuits for the signal and as open circuits for dc. The current source sets the dc current in the drain branch; for the signal it carries no current, so it is treated as an open circuit. RG joins the drain to the gate, so at dc the gate and drain are at the same voltage.

Similar to 7.31 same circuit type, new numbers · Fig. P7.31

Gain of an amplifier with a drain-to-gate feedback resistor, then the effect of a larger bias current.

Similar problem (new numbers)

In the circuit of Fig. P7.31 (a current source I feeding the drain, RG from drain to gate, load RL), the NMOS transistor has Vt=0.6 V and VA=30 V and operates with VD=0.9 V. Take I=0.3 mA, RG=15 MΩ and RL=20 kΩ. What is the voltage gain vo/vi? What do VD and the gain become for I increased to 0.6 mA?

Step 1 · DC bias: VGS and the overdrive

Because IG=0 there is no dc drop across RG, so as in Eq. (7.43) VGS=VDS=VD. The current source forces ID=I.

VOV=VGS−Vt=0.9−0.6=0.30V

VDS=0.9V>VOV, so the transistor is in saturation.

Step 2 · The device and model parameters

From Eq. (7.25), ID=12knVOV2, so kn=2ID/VOV2. From Eq. (7.42) gm=2ID/VOV, and ro=VA/ID:

kn=2(0.3)0.32=6.67mA/V^2,gm=2(0.3)0.30=2.00mA/V,ro=300.3=100kΩ
Step 3 · Small-signal gain

Replace the current source by an open circuit and the transistor by its model (Fig. 7.16(d) with no RD). The load seen by the controlled source is RL′=RL∥ro. From the gain expression after Eq. (7.46):

RL′=20∥100=16.67kΩ
Av=−gmRL′1−1/(gmRG)1+RL′/RG=−2(16.67)1−3.3×10−51+1.1×10−3=−33.3V/V

Check against Eq. (7.47): −gmRL′=−33.3 V/V, the same to three figures.

Step 4 · The current raised to 0.6 mA

The device does not change, so kn=6.67 mA/V² still. Then VOV=2ID/kn and VD=VGS=Vt+VOV:

VOV=2(0.6)6.67=0.424V,VD=0.6+0.424=1.02V
gm=knVOV=2.83mA/V,ro=300.6=50kΩ,RL′=20∥50=14.29kΩ
Av≃−gmRL′=−2.83(14.29)=−40.4V/V
Answers (similar problem)
Gain at 0.3 mA−33.3 V/V
VD at 0.6 mA1.02 V
Gain at 0.6 mA−40.4 V/V

Expansion note: why gm and ro change when the bias current changes

Both are set by the dc bias point: gm grows with the overdrive voltage (or with ID for a given device) and ro=VA/ID falls as the current rises. The book stresses that gm and ro must be recalculated for each bias point.

Small-signal model, gm and ro §7.2.1, pp. 383–387
Quoted · §7.2.1, p. 385

“The most serious shortcoming of the small-signal model of Fig. 7.13(a) is that it assumes the drain current in saturation to be independent of the drain voltage. From our study of the MOSFET characteristics in saturation, we know that the drain current does in fact depend on vDS in a linear manner. Such dependence was modeled by a finite resistance ro between drain and source … where the Early voltage VA=1/λ is a MOSFET parameter that either is specified or can be measured.”

Quoted · pp. 385–386

“We can improve the accuracy of the small-signal model by including ro in parallel with the controlled source, as shown in Fig. 7.13(b). It is important to note that the small-signal model parameters gm and ro depend on the dc bias point of the MOSFET.”

“… replacing the MOSFET with the small-signal model of Fig. 7.13(b) and eliminating the dc sources results in the amplifier small-signal equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 7.14, from which the following expression for the voltage gain can be found:”

Av=−gm(RD∥ro)
(7.39)
Expansion note: what “eliminating the dc sources” does

A dc voltage source holds its terminal at a fixed voltage, so its signal voltage is zero and it is drawn as a short to ground. A dc current source carries a fixed current, so its signal current is zero and it is drawn as an open circuit. The book states this rule on p. 385. Large coupling and bypass capacitors are treated as shorts for signals in the same way.

Summarized · pp. 383–387

The transconductance is gm=knVOV (7.33), also written gm=kn′(W/L)VOV (7.40), gm=2kn′(W/L)ID (7.41) and gm=2ID/VOV (7.42). The book notes that these are different ways of expressing one quantity, so you pick the form that uses the quantities you know. The output resistance ro depends on the dc bias current, so gm and ro must be recomputed whenever the bias point changes.

The DC bias point and the saturation condition §7.2.1, p. 381
Quoted · p. 381

“We can find the dc bias current ID by setting the signal vgs to zero; thus,”

ID=12kn(VGS−Vt)2=12knVOV2
(7.25)

“where we have neglected channel-length modulation (i.e., we have assumed λ=0). Here VOV=VGS−Vt is the overdrive voltage at which the MOSFET is biased to operate. … To ensure saturation-region operation, we must have”

VDS>VOV

Example 7.3: an amplifier with a drain-to-gate feedback resistor pp. 388–392
Quoted · Example 7.3, pp. 388–389

“Figure 7.16(a) shows a discrete MOSFET amplifier biased with a drain-to-gate resistance RG. We will study this biasing arrangement in Section 7.4. The input signal vi is coupled to the gate via a large capacitor, and the output signal at the drain is coupled to the load resistance RL via another large capacitor. We want to analyze this amplifier circuit to determine its small-signal voltage gain, its input resistance, and the largest allowable input signal. The transistor has Vt=1.5 V, kn′(W/L)=0.25 mA/V², and VA=50 V. Assume that the coupling capacitors are large enough that they act as short circuits at the signal frequencies of interest.”

Quoted · p. 390

“We first determine the dc operating point. For this purpose, we eliminate the input signal vi, and open-circuit the two coupling capacitors (since they block dc currents). The result is the circuit shown in Fig. 7.16(b). We note that since IG=0, the dc voltage drop across RG will be zero, and”

VGS=VDS=VDD−RDID
(7.43)

“With VDS=VGS, the NMOS transistor will operate in saturation. Thus,”

ID=12kn(VGS−Vt)2
(7.44)
Quoted · pp. 390–391

“We can determine the values of the transistor small-signal parameters gm and ro by using the dc bias quantities found above …”

“Next we use the equivalent circuit of Fig. 7.16(c) to determine the input resistance Rin≡vi/ii and the voltage gain Av=vo/vi. To that end we simplify the circuit by combining the three parallel resistances ro, RD, and RL in a single resistance RL′ … as shown in Fig. 7.16(d). For the latter circuit we can write the two equations”

vo=(ii−gmvgs)RL′
(7.45)
ii=vgs−voRG
(7.46)

“Substituting for ii from Eq. (7.46) into Eq. (7.45) gives us the following expression for the voltage gain Av≡vo/vi=vo/vgs:”

Av=−gmRL′1−(1/gmRG)1+(RL′/RG)

“Since RG is very large, gmRG≫1 and RL′/RG≪1 (you can easily verify this), the gain expression can be approximated as”

Av≃−gmRL′
(7.47)

“To find the input resistance, we substitute in Eq. (7.46) for vo=Avvgs=−gmRL′vgs, then use Rin≡vi/ii=vgs/ii to get”

Rin=RG1+gmRL′
(7.48)
Expansion note: why RG appears in the gain but can nearly be ignored

RG connects the gate to the drain, so part of the output signal is fed back to the input through it. When RG is in the megohm range the current it carries is tiny compared with gmvgs, so its effect on the gain is very small, which is why the book approximates the gain as −gmRL′. It does, however, reduce the input resistance seen at the gate, as Eq. (7.48) shows.

Problem 7.33 Lesson 17 · pp. 479–480 · §7.2

Verifying the bias and finding the small-signal model and gains of a discrete common-source amplifier with a divider-and-source-resistor bias.

Problem statement

7.33 Figure P7.33 shows a discrete-circuit amplifier. The input signal vsig is coupled to the gate through a very large capacitor (shown as infinite). The transistor source is connected to ground at signal frequencies via a very large capacitor (shown as infinite). The output voltage signal that develops at the drain is coupled to a load resistance via a very large capacitor (shown as infinite). All capacitors behave as short circuits for signals and as open circuits for dc.

  1. If the transistor has Vt=1 V, and kn=4 mA/V², verify that the bias circuit establishes VGS=1.5 V, ID=0.5 mA, and VD=+7.0 V. That is, assume these values, and verify that they are consistent with the values of the circuit components and the device parameters.
  2. Find gm and ro if VA=100 V.
  3. Draw a complete small-signal equivalent circuit for the amplifier, assuming all capacitors behave as short circuits at signal frequencies.
  4. Find Rin, vgs/vsig, vo/vgs, and vo/vsig.
Expansion note: how to read the capacitor symbols

“Shown as infinite” means each capacitor is treated as an ideal short circuit for the signal. For dc it blocks current, so for the dc bias you remove (open-circuit) every capacitor and the source vsig. This gives one circuit for the bias and another for the signal.

Similar to 7.33 same circuit type, new numbers · Fig. P7.33

Verify the bias of a discrete CS amplifier, find its small-signal parameters, draw its model and find its gains.

Similar problem (new numbers)

Fig. P7.33 shows a discrete-circuit amplifier of the same form, with these values: VDD=12 V, RG1=23 MΩ, RG2=7 MΩ, RD=15 kΩ, RS=5 kΩ, load RL=20 kΩ and source resistance Rsig=250 kΩ. All capacitors behave as short circuits for signals and as open circuits for dc.

  1. If the transistor has Vt=0.8 V and kn=2.4 mA/V², verify that the bias circuit establishes VGS=1.3 V, ID=0.3 mA and VD=+7.5 V.
  2. Find gm and ro if VA=80 V.
  3. Draw a complete small-signal equivalent circuit for the amplifier.
  4. Find Rin, vgs/vsig, vo/vgs, and vo/vsig.
Step 1 · (a) Check the dc bias

Gate voltage from the unloaded divider (the gate draws no current): VG=VDDRG2/(RG1+RG2)=12(7)/30=2.80 V. With the given values:

ID=12kn(VGS−Vt)2=12(2.4)(1.3−0.8)2=0.30mA✓
VS=IDRS=0.3(5)=1.50V,VG=VGS+VS=1.3+1.5=2.80V✓(7.137)
VD=VDD−IDRD=12−0.3(15)=7.50V✓

Saturation: VDS=VD−VS=6.0 V >VOV=0.5 V.

Step 2 · (b) gm and ro
gm=knVOV=2.4(0.5)=1.20mA/V(7.33),ro=VAID=800.3=267kΩ
Step 3 · (c) The small-signal equivalent circuit

Short the coupling and bypass capacitors and ground VDD. The result has the form of Fig. 7.57(c): vsig and Rsig feed the gate node, where RG1 and RG2 both go to ground; between gate G and source S (at ground) sit vgs and the controlled source gmvgs in parallel with ro; the drain node connects to ground through RD and, in parallel, through RL, giving vo. RS is shorted by its bypass capacitor and does not appear.

Step 4 · (d) Gains

By inspection of the circuit of Step 3, as in Fig. 7.57(c):

Rin=RG1∥RG2=23∥7=5.37MΩ(7.149)
vgsvsig=RinRin+Rsig=53675367+250=0.955
RD∥RL∥ro=15∥20∥267=8.30kΩ,vovgs=−gm(RD∥RL∥ro)=−1.2(8.30)=−9.97V/V
vovsig=0.955×(−9.97)=−9.52V/V(7.150)
Answers (similar problem)
(a) checkVGS = 1.3 V, ID = 0.3 mA, VD = 7.5 V are consistent
(b)gm = 1.20 mA/V, ro = 267 kΩ
(c)Model of the form of Fig. 7.57(c); RS bypassed
(d) Rin5.37 MΩ
(d) vgs/vsig0.955
(d) vo/vgs−9.97 V/V
(d) vo/vsig−9.52 V/V

Expansion note: what “verify” means in part (a)

Part (a) lets you assume the bias values and checks whether they satisfy every relation of the circuit at once: the divider, the source-resistor constraint, the drain drop and the device equation. If one relation fails, the assumed values are not the bias point of this circuit.

Biasing by fixing VG and a source resistance §7.4.1, pp. 449–451
Quoted · p. 449

“An excellent biasing technique for discrete MOSFET circuits consists of fixing the dc voltage at the gate, VG, and connecting a resistance in the source lead, as shown in Fig. 7.50(a). For this circuit,”

VG=VGS+RSID
(7.137)
Quoted · p. 451

“Now, if VG is much greater than VGS, ID will be mostly determined by the values of VG and RS. However, even if VG is not much larger than VGS, resistor RS provides negative feedback, which acts to stabilize the value of the bias current ID.”

“The circuit in Fig. 7.50(c) uses one power-supply VDD and derives VG through a voltage divider (RG1, RG2). Since IG=0, RG1 and RG2 can be selected to be very large (in the megohm range), allowing the MOSFET to present a large input resistance to a signal source …”

Expansion note: why RS stabilizes the current

If ID rises, the drop RSID rises too. With VG fixed by the divider, Eq. (7.137) then forces VGS down, which pulls ID back. The effect is stronger when RSID is a larger part of VG.

Example 7.11: a worked bias design and analysis §7.4.1, pp. 451–453
Summarized · pp. 451–453

The example designs the circuit of Fig. 7.50(c) for a given ID and checks the effect of replacing the transistor by one with a different Vt. The method: choose voltage drops across RD and RS (the book’s rule of thumb is one-third of VDD across each of RD, the transistor and RS), get the resistors from R=V/ID, find VOV from ID=12kn′(W/L)VOV2, then VGS=Vt+VOV and VG=VS+VGS, and finally choose megohm-range divider resistors for that VG.

The CS amplifier with classical biasing §7.5.1, pp. 461–463
Quoted · pp. 461–463

“Notice that to establish a signal ground (sometimes called an ac ground) at the source, we have connected a large capacitor, CS, between the source and ground. This capacitor, usually in the microfarad range, is required to provide a very small impedance (ideally, zero impedance—in effect, a short circuit) at all signal frequencies of interest. In this way, the signal current passes through CS to ground and thus bypasses the resistance RS; hence, CS is called a bypass capacitor.”

“Since a capacitor behaves as an open circuit at dc, the circuit for performing the dc bias design and analysis is obtained by open-circuiting all capacitors. … To determine the characteristics of the CS amplifier of Fig. 7.57(a)—that is, its input resistance, voltage gain, and output resistance—we replace the MOSFET with its hybrid-π small-signal model, replace VDD with a signal ground, and replace all coupling and bypass capacitors with short circuits. The result is the circuit in Fig. 7.57(c). Analysis is straightforward and is shown on the figure, thus”

Rin=RG1∥RG2
(7.149)

“… The overall voltage gain Gv is”

Gv=−RinRin+Rsiggm(RD∥RL∥ro)
(7.150)
Expansion note: what the signal-only circuit keeps and discards

The signal circuit keeps the transistor model, every resistor that touches a signal node (Rsig, RG1, RG2, RD, RL) and the signal source. It discards the supply (now ground), every capacitor (now a short) and any resistor whose signal path to ground is shorted by a bypass capacitor.

Small-signal model, gm and ro §7.2.1, pp. 383–387
Quoted · §7.2.1, p. 385

“The most serious shortcoming of the small-signal model of Fig. 7.13(a) is that it assumes the drain current in saturation to be independent of the drain voltage. From our study of the MOSFET characteristics in saturation, we know that the drain current does in fact depend on vDS in a linear manner. Such dependence was modeled by a finite resistance ro between drain and source … where the Early voltage VA=1/λ is a MOSFET parameter that either is specified or can be measured.”

Quoted · pp. 385–386

“We can improve the accuracy of the small-signal model by including ro in parallel with the controlled source, as shown in Fig. 7.13(b). It is important to note that the small-signal model parameters gm and ro depend on the dc bias point of the MOSFET.”

“… replacing the MOSFET with the small-signal model of Fig. 7.13(b) and eliminating the dc sources results in the amplifier small-signal equivalent circuit shown in Fig. 7.14, from which the following expression for the voltage gain can be found:”

Av=−gm(RD∥ro)
(7.39)
Expansion note: what “eliminating the dc sources” does

A dc voltage source holds its terminal at a fixed voltage, so its signal voltage is zero and it is drawn as a short to ground. A dc current source carries a fixed current, so its signal current is zero and it is drawn as an open circuit. The book states this rule on p. 385. Large coupling and bypass capacitors are treated as shorts for signals in the same way.

Summarized · pp. 383–387

The transconductance is gm=knVOV (7.33), also written gm=kn′(W/L)VOV (7.40), gm=2kn′(W/L)ID (7.41) and gm=2ID/VOV (7.42). The book notes that these are different ways of expressing one quantity, so you pick the form that uses the quantities you know. The output resistance ro depends on the dc bias current, so gm and ro must be recomputed whenever the bias point changes.

Problem 7.64 Lesson 17 · p. 485 · §7.3

Overall voltage gain of a common-source amplifier with a given source resistance, load and drain resistor.

Problem statement

7.64 Calculate the overall voltage gain of a CS amplifier fed with a 1-MΩ source and connected to a 20-kΩ load. The MOSFET has gm=2 mA/V, and a drain resistance RD=20 kΩ is utilized.

No figure is referenced by this problem. The reading’s Fig. 7.36 shows the amplifier type; it is included in the reading panels below.

Expansion note: what “overall” gain means

The book distinguishes the voltage gain of the amplifier proper, Av=vo/vi, from the overall voltage gain Gv=vo/vsig, which also includes any loss at the input between the signal source and the amplifier input. Whether the two differ depends on the amplifier’s input resistance.

Similar to 7.64 same amplifier type, new numbers · Fig. 7.36

Overall voltage gain of a common-source amplifier fed from a resistive source and driving a load.

Similar problem (new numbers)

Calculate the overall voltage gain of a CS amplifier fed with a 500-kΩ source and connected to a 10-kΩ load. The MOSFET has gm=4 mA/V, and a drain resistance RD=15 kΩ is utilized.

Step 1 · Input resistance and the input divider

By inspection of Fig. 7.36(b), as in Eq. (7.87), Rin=∞, so no signal current flows through Rsig and vi=vsig whatever the value of Rsig (Eq. (7.83) with Rin→∞).

Step 2 · Open-circuit gain and output resistance
Avo=−gmRD=−4(15)=−60V/V(7.88),Ro=RD=15kΩ(7.89)
Step 3 · Load connected

Eq. (7.90), then the equivalent form (7.91):

Av=AvoRLRL+Ro=−601010+15=−24.0V/V
Av=−gm(RD∥RL)=−4(15∥10)=−4(6.0)=−24.0V/V
Step 4 · Overall gain

With vi=vsig, Eq. (7.92) gives Gv=Av:

Gv=vovsig=−gm(RD∥RL)=−24.0V/V

Check: the two forms of Step 3 agree, as the book says they must.

Answers (similar problem)
Rin∞
Avo−60 V/V
Ro15 kΩ
Av−24.0 V/V
Gv−24.0 V/V

Characterizing amplifiers §7.3.2, pp. 419–421
Quoted · pp. 419–420

“Figure 7.35(a) shows an amplifier fed with a signal source that has an open-circuit voltage vsig and an internal resistance Rsig. These can be the parameters of an actual signal source or, in a cascade amplifier, the Thévenin equivalent of the output circuit of another amplifier stage preceding the one under study. The amplifier is shown with a load resistance RL connected to the output terminal. … Figure 7.35(b) shows the amplifier circuit with the amplifier block replaced by its equivalent-circuit model. The input resistance Rin represents the loading effect of the amplifier input on the signal source.”

Quoted · p. 421

“… together with the resistance Rsig forms a voltage divider that reduces vsig to the value vi that appears at the amplifier input,”

vi=RinRin+Rsigvsig
(7.83)

“The second parameter in characterizing amplifier performance is the open-circuit voltage gain Avo … The third and final parameter is the output resistance Ro. Observe from Fig. 7.35(b) that Ro is the resistance seen looking back into the amplifier output terminal with vi set to zero.”

vo=RLRL+RoAvovi
(7.84)

“Thus the voltage gain of the amplifier proper, Av, can be found from”

Av≡vovi=AvoRLRL+Ro
(7.85)

“and the overall voltage gain, Gv≡vo/vsig, can be determined by combining Eqs. (7.83) and (7.85):”

Gv=RinRin+RsigAvoRLRL+Ro
(7.86)
Expansion note: the order of the three characteristic parameters

Rin is found with the output unconnected, Avo with the load removed, and Ro with the input source set to zero. Each is a property of the amplifier alone; the source and load enter only when the three are combined in Eqs. (7.83) to (7.86).

The common-source amplifier: characteristic parameters §7.3.3, pp. 422–423
Quoted · pp. 422–423

“Figure 7.36(a) shows a common-source amplifier (with the biasing arrangement omitted) fed with a signal source vsig having a source resistance Rsig. We want to analyze this circuit to determine Rin, Avo, and Ro. For this purpose, we assume that RD is part of the amplifier; thus if a load resistance RL is connected to the amplifier output, RL appears in parallel with RD. In such a case, we want to determine Av and Gv as well. Replacing the MOSFET with its hybrid-π model (without ro), we obtain the CS amplifier equivalent circuit in Fig. 7.36(b) for which, tracing the signal from input to output, we can write by inspection”

Rin=∞,vi=vsig,vgs=vi,vo=−gmvgsRD
(7.87)

“Thus,”

Avo≡vovi=−gmRD
(7.88)
Ro=RD
(7.89)

“If a load resistance RL is connected across RD, the voltage gain Av can be obtained from”

Av=AvoRLRL+Ro
(7.90)

“… or alternatively by simply adding RL in parallel with RD in Eq. (7.88), thus”

Av=−gm(RD∥RL)
(7.91)

“We can easily show that the expression obtained from Eq. (7.90) is identical to that in Eq. (7.91). Finally, since Rin=∞ and thus vi=vsig, the overall voltage gain Gv is equal to Av,”

Gv≡vovsig=−gm(RD∥RL)
(7.92)
Expansion note: why a controlled-source model gives an infinite input resistance

In the model the input terminals G and S see an open circuit: the controlled source is on the output side and the gate carries no current. A source resistor Rsig in series with an open circuit carries no current, so it drops no voltage. The book writes “Rin=∞” for this reason (Eq. (7.87)).

Related exercises in the reading p. 423
Related exercise in the reading · p. 423

7.21 A CS amplifier utilizes a MOSFET biased at ID=0.25 mA with VOV=0.25 V and RD=20 kΩ. The amplifier is fed with a signal source having Rsig=100 kΩ, and a 20-kΩ load is connected to the output. Find Rin, Avo, Ro, Av, and Gv. If, to maintain reasonable linearity, the peak of the input sine-wave signal is limited to 10% of 2VOV, what is the peak of the sine-wave voltage at the output?

Book answers: ∞; −40 V/V; 20 kΩ; −20 V/V; −20 V/V; 1 V
